did_you_know.text: Did you know? Micah describes injustice that is planned in advance: the wicked plot it at night and carry it out in the morning because they have the power to do so.
Did you know? The sin described is not merely an evil thought, but the seizure of fields, houses, people, and inheritances—harming both property and families.

Did you know? The punishment is described in words that mirror the oppressors’ actions: just as they planned harm against others, so the Lord plans disaster against this family; they will no longer walk proudly.
Did you know? On the day of calamity, a public lament will be heard over the loss of the land, and the people will describe how their inheritance was taken and divided among others.
Did you know? The loss of the inheritance is also emphasized through the term “measuring line”: no one will remain to measure out and assign himself a plot of land among the assembly of the Lord.
Did you know? Micah rejects the claim that the Lord’s words are harsh to everyone. He declares that the Lord’s words bring good to the upright person who walks in the right way.
Did you know? Micah accuses the people of treating those who pass by peacefully like enemies, even stripping them of their clothing and possessions.
Did you know? The oppression especially harms women and children: women are driven from their homes, and children lose the honor and security they once had.
Did you know? The land, which is supposed to be a place of rest, is described as a place that provides no rest because defilement and sin bring destruction upon it.
Did you know? The people prefer a preacher who speaks about wine and strong drink, and Micah presents this as an example of false spiritual leadership that flatters its listeners.
Did you know? At the end of the chapter there is also a promise of gathering: the Lord will bring Jacob together with the remnant of Israel, like sheep being gathered into a flock.
Did you know? The final verse portrays the Lord as the leader at the head of the people: “the one who breaks through” opens the way, and the King goes before them all.
